patient.name: Doreen Campbell
patient.complaint: Found by her daughter drowsy and confused after 4 days of feeling unwell
background: Type 2 diabetes on metformin and gliclazide
Burning on passing urine for a week

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with an older type 2 diabetic, confused and dry, glucose above 30 and osmolality above 320 but a near-normal pH: the absence of acidosis is what separates HHS from DKA.

points: Days of **thirst and passing lots of urine**, then drowsy.
Dysuria for a week; barely drinking.
Very dry tongue, sunken eyes; responds to voice.

steps.lead: Doreen's confusion, **reduced GCS**, dry mucous membranes, hypotension and tachycardia are all **profound volume depletion**.

steps.title: First bloods
steps.text: Huge glucose, high sodium and urea, but **pH and bicarbonate normal** and ketones minimal.

steps.lead: Doreen meets the triad: glucose **above 30**, osmolality **above 320** and volume depletion, with pH above 7.3 and HCO3 above 15.
Doreen has the classic triggers: an **infection** (urinary), **dehydration** and a **diuretic** (furosemide).

steps.q: Doreen's glucose is 46 with pH 7.36 and ketones 0.6. Which is most likely?
steps.r: Glucose above 30 and osmolality above 320 **without acidosis** is HHS. DKA needs ketones above 3 and acidosis.

steps.lead: Doreen's **normal pH** is the single result that makes this HHS rather than DKA.
Two dangers lie ahead for Doreen: **cerebral oedema** if she is corrected too fast, and **thrombosis** from her thick, hyperosmolar blood.

steps.text: A 'mildly raised' ketone of 0.6 to 1 does not make it DKA. HHS allows minimal ketones; DKA needs ketonaemia above 3 with acidosis.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' (glucose, osmolality, ketones and a venous gas) or a calculation of osmolality from sodium, glucose and urea.

steps.lead: Doreen's glucose is **46** and her calculated osmolality **376**; ketones and pH confirm there is **no significant acidosis**.

steps.text: Calculated osmolality = **(2 × Na) + glucose + urea**. Doreen: (2 × 154) + 46 + 22 = 376 mOsm/kg.

steps.q: Which set of tests should Doreen have straight away?
o: U&Es, venous gas, FBC and CRP
steps.r: **U&Es, VBG and FBC/CRP** assess electrolytes, acid-base and the infective trigger. HbA1c helps later, not now.

steps.lead: Doreen's tests look for the **trigger**: her CRP of 168 and WCC of 15 fit the urinary infection.

steps.title: Trigger and complications screen
steps.text: Pre-renal AKI from dehydration and a **urinary infection** as the trigger. Also do an ECG and blood cultures.

visual.title: Doreen's venous pH
visual.label: Doreen 7.36
visual.caption: Above 7.3: no significant acidosis, so HHS, not DKA.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (IV 0.9% saline, before insulin) or 'next step' questions on low-dose insulin, potassium or a falling GCS from cerebral oedema.

steps.r: **IV 0.9% saline first**: fluids alone lower glucose and osmolality. Insulin comes later, at a low dose.

steps.lead: Doreen gets **1 litre of 0.9% saline over 1 to 2 hours**, then more. Fluids come **before insulin**.

visual.title: Doreen's first 24 hours
visual.caption: Osmolality 376 → 300 over 24 hours (about 3 per hour): a slow, safe fall. Glucose falls under 5 mmol/L per hour.

steps.lead: Once Doreen is resuscitated and her glucose stops falling with fluids, **low-dose IV insulin** starts; her **potassium** is checked and replaced.

steps.title: Doreen's HHS pathway
nodes: IV 0.9% saline, 1 L over 1–2 h, then continue
Monitor glucose, osmolality, sodium, potassium hourly
Treat the trigger: antibiotics for her UTI
steps.caption: Slow and steady: the aim is gradual correction, not speed.

steps.lead: Doreen's **UTI** is treated with antibiotics. Her correction stays **gradual**; a falling GCS would mean calling ITU about **mannitol**.
Doreen's plan follows the **JBDS HHS guideline**: fluids first, low-dose insulin, gradual correction, VTE prophylaxis.

steps.text: Do not start insulin first or at the DKA rate. Insulin before fluids drives glucose and water into cells and can cause **circulatory collapse**.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why there is no ketosis (relative insulin deficiency), why dehydration is so severe (osmotic diuresis), why rapid correction causes cerebral oedema, or why thrombosis risk is high.

steps.lead: Doreen still makes **some insulin**: enough to stop lipolysis and ketones, not enough to control her glucose.

steps.q: Why does Doreen have no significant ketoacidosis?
o: Her kidneys excrete all the ketones
Relative insulin deficiency still suppresses lipolysis
steps.r: **Relative, not absolute,** insulin deficiency: a little insulin switches off ketogenesis. DKA is near-absolute deficiency.

steps.lead: Doreen's glucose spilled into her urine, pulling water with it (**osmotic diuresis**). Dehydration then cut her kidney function, raising glucose further.

steps.title: The vicious cycle
nodes: Osmotic diuresis: water lost in urine

steps.lead: Over days, water left Doreen's brain cells. If her osmolality fell fast, water would rush back in: **cerebral oedema**.
Doreen's thick, hyperosmolar blood raises her risk of **stroke, MI and VTE**, so she gets prophylactic heparin.

visual.title: Safe rate of osmolality fall
visual.label: Doreen 3.2
visual.caption: JBDS target is a fall of 3 to 8 mOsm/kg per hour.

mcq.q: HHS typically occurs in which patients?
mcq.r: HHS is a **type 2** emergency, usually in older people.

mcq.q: Which glucose cut-off is in the HHS triad?

mcq.r: HHS has **no significant ketoacidosis** (pH above 7.3, HCO3 above 15).
Rapid osmolality fall shifts water into brain cells: **cerebral oedema**.

mcq.q: Which osmolality cut-off is in the HHS triad?
What is given first in HHS?
Cerebral oedema develops during treatment. What next?
o: Contact ITU about mannitol and hypertonic saline
mcq.r: Call **ITU** regarding mannitol infusion and hypertonic saline.

mcq.q: Why is there no significant ketosis in HHS?
mcq.r: Enough insulin remains to **suppress lipolysis and ketogenesis**.

mcq.q: Why is dehydration so profound in HHS?
mcq.r: Glucose in the urine drags water: **osmotic diuresis**.

technique.stem: An 82 year old man with type 2 diabetes is brought from his care home with a 5 day history of increasing drowsiness and reduced fluid intake. He has a cough. His mucous membranes are dry. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 116 bpm, BP 88/52 mmHg and respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question: hyperglycaemic emergency, so DKA or HHS?
Older type 2 diabetic, slow onset over days, severely dry and shocked.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Glucose 52, osmolality (2 × 151) + 52 + 24 = 378, pH 7.34, ketones minimal: **HHS**.

elim: Low sodium and high potassium; sodium is high here.
Needs ketones above 3 and pH below 7.3; both are near normal.
Glucose is 52.
Drowsiness here is explained by hyperosmolality and dehydration.

steps.x: **C. Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state.** pH 7.34 and ketones 0.8 = no significant acidosis.

technique.stem: A 76 year old woman with type 2 diabetes is confused and dehydrated after a week of diarrhoea. Her capillary glucose reads 'HI'. Her pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 96/58 mmHg. Her venous pH is 7.37 and blood ketones are 0.4 mmol/L.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnostic test question: which result completes the triad?
Very high glucose, no acidosis, no ketones: likely HHS.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Confirm hyperosmolality: **serum osmolality above 320** (measured or calculated).

elim: Look for a trigger; do not make the diagnosis.
Confusion is explained metabolically; not the confirmatory test.
Reflects 3 months of control, not the acute state.
Looks for a trigger; she has diarrhoea, not urinary symptoms.

steps.x: **D. Serum osmolality.** Glucose >30 + osmolality >320 + no acidosis = HHS.

technique.stem: A 74 year old man with HHS has received 3 litres of intravenous 0.9% saline over 6 hours. His glucose has fallen from 48 to 30 mmol/L and his osmolality is falling steadily. His pulse rate is 94 bpm and BP 122/70 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Add potassium chloride to the intravenous fluids

steps.x: Next step: what is wrong right now?
Fluids are working, but potassium is **3.1**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Electrolytes, particularly **potassium**, must be corrected alongside fluids.

elim: There is no acidosis in HHS.
Glucose is still falling with fluids; and 0.1 is the DKA rate. Insulin would also drop potassium further.
He is still hyperosmolar and needs ongoing fluids.
Only once glucose falls below about 14 mmol/L.

steps.x: **A. Add potassium chloride to the intravenous fluids.** Correct potassium alongside.

technique.stem: An 80 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has a 10 day history of polyuria and thirst, followed by confusion. Her glucose is 50 mmol/L, sodium 152 mmol/L and urea 26 mmol/L. Her pulse rate is 120 bpm and BP 86/50 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her severe dehydration?
o: Third-space fluid loss into the gut

steps.x: A mechanism question: why is she so dry?
Polyuria came first, then dehydration.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Glucose in the urine drags water: **osmotic diuresis**, a self-reinforcing cycle.

elim: No diarrhoea in the history.
Would retain water and lower sodium.
Seen in obstruction or pancreatitis, not here.
HHS has minimal ketones.

steps.x: **C. Osmotic diuresis from glycosuria.** Hyperglycaemia → polyuria → dehydration.

practice.stem: A 77 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has a 6 day history of thirst, polyuria and increasing confusion. She has had dysuria. Her mucous membranes are dry. Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 114 bpm, BP 94/56 mmHg and respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Glucose 44, calculated osmolality (2 × 150) + 44 + 20 = 364, normal pH and no ketones in an older type 2 diabetic: HHS. DKA needs ketones above 3 and acidosis.

steps.x: Diagnosis: hyperglycaemic emergency, so check ketones and pH.
Older type 2, slow onset, urinary trigger, dehydrated.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Glucose above 30, osmolality 364, no acidosis: **HHS**.

elim: pH and ketones are normal.
Glucose is 44.
pH is normal.
Urea of 20 is pre-renal; the hyperosmolality explains the confusion.

steps.x: **B. Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state.** Glucose >30, osmolality >320, no acidosis.

practice.stem: An 84 year old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin is found drowsy at home. He has had a burning sensation passing urine and offensive urine for 5 days. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 120 bpm and BP 90/54 mmHg. His glucose is 49 mmol/L and osmolality 362 mOsm/kg with no acidosis.
practice.q: Which is the most likely precipitant?
practice.e: Infection is the commonest trigger of HHS; dysuria, offensive urine, fever and high inflammatory markers point to a UTI. Gliclazide overdose causes hypoglycaemia.

steps.x: A precipitant question: what tipped him into HHS?
HHS (glucose 49, osmolality 362, no acidosis) with urinary symptoms and fever.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urinary tract infection**: infection is the classic trigger.

elim: Causes alcoholic ketoacidosis or hypoglycaemia.
Causes hypoglycaemia, not hyperglycaemia.
Not a trigger of HHS.
Lowers glucose; may cause ketosis, not HHS.

steps.x: **E. Urinary tract infection.** Triggers: infection, dehydration, steroids, diuretics.

practice.stem: A 72 year old man with type 2 diabetes was started on a high-dose oral medicine for an exacerbation of COPD 6 days ago. He is now confused and very thirsty. His pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 102/60 mmHg. His glucose is 41 mmol/L, osmolality 338 mOsm/kg and pH 7.37.
practice.q: Which drug most likely precipitated his condition?
practice.e: Steroids raise glucose through insulin resistance and gluconeogenesis and are a classic HHS trigger, as are diuretics. A COPD exacerbation is treated with oral prednisolone.

steps.x: A drug cause question: which drug raises glucose?
HHS (glucose 41, osmolality 338, normal pH) after COPD treatment.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: COPD exacerbation = **oral prednisolone**: steroids trigger HHS.

elim: Does not raise glucose meaningfully.
Small glucose effect; not an acute trigger.
Can mask hypoglycaemia; not an HHS trigger.
Not a trigger, and not a COPD treatment.

steps.x: **E. Prednisolone.** Steroids and diuretics are the drug triggers.

practice.stem: A 70 year old woman with type 2 diabetes is confused and severely dehydrated. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 96/60 mmHg. The admitting doctor is deciding between diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state.
practice.q: Which finding most strongly supports a diagnosis of hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state?
practice.e: HHS and DKA both cause severe hyperglycaemia and dehydration; the absence of significant acidosis (pH above 7.3, HCO3 above 15, minimal ketones) defines HHS.

steps.x: A distinguishing-feature question: what is present in one and not the other?

clues: deciding between diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state
steps.x: Both cause confusion, dehydration and high glucose.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **No significant acidosis**: pH 7.36, HCO3 21, ketones 0.7.

elim: Occurs in both.
Occurs in both (HHS needs above 30).
Occurs in both from dehydration.
Occurs in both.

steps.x: **A. Absence of significant acidosis.** The one feature that separates HHS from DKA.

practice.stem: A 78 year old woman is being treated for HHS. Over the first 6 hours her osmolality has fallen from 370 to 320 mOsm/kg. She now has a headache, vomits and becomes more drowsy. Her pulse rate is 58 bpm and BP 168/94 mmHg. Her sodium and potassium are stable.
practice.q: Which is the most likely complication?
practice.e: A fall of about 8 mOsm/kg per hour is too fast; water shifts into brain cells, causing cerebral oedema with headache, vomiting, drowsiness and a Cushing response.

steps.x: A complication question: what happened during treatment?

clues: headache, vomits and becomes more drowsy
pulse rate is 58 bpm and BP 168/94 mmHg
steps.x: Osmolality fell 50 in 6 hours (over 8 per hour); signs of raised intracranial pressure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Rapid correction: **cerebral oedema**.

elim: Follows rapid sodium correction; her sodium is stable.
Not suggested; would not cause bradycardia and hypertension.
Causes weakness and arrhythmias, not raised ICP.
Sudden thunderclap headache; the timing fits over-rapid correction.

steps.x: **B. Cerebral oedema.** Correct osmolality gradually (3–8 per hour).

practice.stem: An 81 year old man is on day 3 of treatment for HHS. He has new swelling and pain in his left calf. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 132/78 mmHg. His left calf is 4 cm larger than the right and tender. He was not prescribed heparin on admission.
practice.q: Which is the most likely complication?
practice.e: Hyperosmolar states cause hyperviscosity and predispose to thrombosis (VTE, stroke, MI), which is why prophylactic LMWH is given. A unilateral swollen tender calf is a DVT.

steps.x: A complication question: link the new sign to HHS.
Unilateral swollen tender calf in a hyperosmolar patient with no prophylaxis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: HHS predisposes to **thrombosis**: **DVT**.

elim: Would show spreading redness and fever.
Follows trauma or ischaemia, with severe pain on stretch.
Chronic, painless and often bilateral.
Needs a known knee cyst; DVT must be excluded first anyway.

steps.x: **C. Deep vein thrombosis.** Hyperviscosity = thrombosis; give LMWH prophylaxis.

practice.stem: A 79 year old woman with type 2 diabetes is drowsy and dehydrated. Her pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 98/60 mmHg. Her venous pH is 7.36.
practice.q: What is her calculated serum osmolality?
practice.e: (2 × 150) + 40 + 20 = 360 mOsm/kg, above the 320 cut-off, confirming hyperosmolality.

steps.x: A calculation: use the formula from the notes.
Probable HHS; you need the osmolality.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: You forgot to double the sodium.
A normal value; you left out glucose and urea partly.
Arithmetic error.
Too high; you may have doubled glucose.

steps.x: **D. 360 mOsm/kg.** (2 × Na) + glucose + urea.

practice.stem: An 83 year old woman with type 2 diabetes is brought in confused with a capillary glucose of 'HI'. Her temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 116 bpm and BP 92/56 mmHg. She is very dry. Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state is suspected.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation to distinguish it from diabetic ketoacidosis?
o: Blood ketones and venous blood gas
practice.e: Ketones and a VBG show whether there is significant ketoacidosis; their absence confirms HHS rather than DKA. U&Es and FBC/CRP are sent at the same time.

steps.x: A 'distinguish' question: what separates HHS from DKA?
The difference is acidosis and ketones.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Blood ketones and a venous blood gas**.

elim: Does not separate HHS from DKA.
Shows long-term control only.
For pancreatitis.
Looks for the trigger, not the diagnosis.

steps.x: **A. Blood ketones and venous blood gas.** No acidosis = HHS.

practice.stem: An 80 year old man with type 2 diabetes is confused and dehydrated. His pulse rate is 118 bpm, BP 88/50 mmHg and respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute. His glucose is 48 mmol/L, calculated osmolality 368 mOsm/kg, pH 7.36 and blood ketones 0.4 mmol/L.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: HHS is treated with IV 0.9% saline first (about 1 litre over 1 to 2 hours), which lowers osmolality and glucose. Insulin is started later at a low dose.

steps.x: Initial management of HHS.
HHS: glucose 48, osmolality 368, no acidosis, shocked.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV 0.9% saline** first, before insulin.

elim: Adds glucose; used only once glucose has fallen.
Fluids come before insulin in HHS.
There is no acidosis.
He is shocked and confused; he needs IV fluid.

steps.x: **A. Intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride.** Fluids before insulin.

practice.stem: A 75 year old woman with HHS has received 4 litres of intravenous 0.9% saline over 8 hours. She is now well perfused. Her glucose has stopped falling and remains at 32 mmol/L. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 128/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Intravenous insulin at a low fixed rate
practice.e: Once fully fluid-resuscitated and glucose no longer falls with fluids alone, low-dose IV insulin (0.05 units/kg/hour) is started, with potassium monitored.

steps.x: Next step: fluids are done, what comes second?
Resuscitated, potassium fine, glucose plateaued at 32.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Low-dose IV insulin**.

elim: Would worsen dehydration.
No acidosis.
Too slow for an emergency.
Not the acute treatment.

steps.x: **B. Intravenous insulin at a low fixed rate.** Insulin only after fluids.

practice.stem: A 77 year old man is being treated for HHS with intravenous fluids and insulin. Ten hours in, his osmolality has fallen by 90 mOsm/kg. He becomes increasingly drowsy and his GCS falls from 14 to 9. His pulse rate is 54 bpm and BP 172/96 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Intensive care review for mannitol and hypertonic saline
practice.e: Over-rapid correction has caused cerebral oedema. Contact ITU regarding mannitol infusion and hypertonic saline. Lumbar puncture is dangerous with raised intracranial pressure.

steps.x: A next-step question: what has happened, and who manages it?

clues: pulse rate is 54 bpm and BP 172/96 mmHg
steps.x: 9 mOsm/kg per hour (too fast) with a falling GCS and Cushing response: **cerebral oedema**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Contact **ITU** about **mannitol** and hypertonic saline.

elim: Would lower osmolality even faster.
More fluid worsens the osmotic shift.
Used for tumour oedema, not osmotic cerebral oedema.
Risks coning with raised intracranial pressure.

steps.x: **C. Intensive care review for mannitol and hypertonic saline.**

practice.stem: A 74 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has HHS with a glucose of 45 mmol/L. Her pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 96/58 mmHg. Her blood ketones are 0.5 mmol/L and venous pH is 7.37. A student asks why she has no ketoacidosis.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
practice.e: In HHS enough insulin remains to suppress lipolysis and ketogenesis but not enough to control glucose. DKA results from near-absolute insulin deficiency.

steps.x: A mechanism question: why no ketones?
Type 2 diabetics still make some insulin.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Relative insulin deficiency**: enough to block lipolysis and ketogenesis.

elim: That causes DKA.
Glucagon promotes ketogenesis, not prevents it.
Ketones are not being made in the first place.
Ketones are minimal, not buffered.

steps.x: **E. Relative insulin deficiency suppressing lipolysis.**

prompts.q: What is HHS and what is its diagnostic triad, with cut-offs?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: all three, plus no acidosis.

points.p: No significant ketoacidosis: pH above 7.3, HCO3 above 15

prompts.q: Who gets HHS and what triggers it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: find the trigger in the stem.

points.why: May be the first presentation of diabetes.
Elderly people who cannot drink enough.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: dehydration and a reduced GCS.

points.p: Confusion or altered consciousness; reduced GCS

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one feature decides it.

points.p: Absence of significant acidosis in HHS

prompts.q: What are the complications of HHS and its treatment?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: falling GCS during treatment = cerebral oedema.

points.p: Cerebral oedema from rapid correction of osmolality
points.why: Keep the fall to 3–8 mOsm/kg per hour.

points.p: If it occurs, contact ITU about mannitol and hypertonic saline
points.why: Do not just speed up the fluids.

prompts.q: Which investigations confirm HHS and look for the trigger?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: glucose, osmolality, ketones, gas.

points.p: Ketones minimal, pH normal or mildly low

prompts.q: What is the order of treatment in HHS?

points.p: IV 0.9% saline first, e.g. 1 litre over 1–2 hours
points.why: Fluids alone lower glucose and osmolality.

prompts.q: What else must be done in the emergency management of HHS?

points.p: Treat the precipitant: infection, MI, stroke
points.why: Antibiotics for the UTI or pneumonia.

points.p: Cerebral oedema: contact ITU about mannitol and hypertonic saline
points.why: Watch for headache and falling GCS.

prompts.q: Why is there no ketoacidosis, and why is dehydration so severe?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: relative insulin deficiency and osmotic diuresis.

points.p: Enough insulin to suppress lipolysis and ketogenesis, not hyperglycaemia
points.why: Insulin's anti-lipolytic effect needs less insulin.
Water follows glucose into the urine.

points.p: Dehydration causes pre-renal impairment, worsening hyperglycaemia

prompts.q: Why does rapid correction cause cerebral oedema, and why is thrombosis common?

points.p: High osmolality draws water out of brain cells
Rapid correction shifts water back into cells quickly
points.why: Hence the 3–8 mOsm/kg per hour target.

glossary.HHS: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state: very high glucose and osmolality with dehydration but no significant acidosis.
glossary.DKA: Diabetic ketoacidosis: hyperglycaemia, ketones above 3 and acidosis, usually in type 1 diabetes.
glossary.osmolality: Concentration of dissolved particles in blood; normal 275–295 mOsm/kg.
glossary.serum osmolality: Measured particle concentration of serum; above 320 mOsm/kg in HHS.
glossary.hyperosmolality: Abnormally concentrated blood, which pulls water out of cells.
glossary.mOsm/kg: Milliosmoles per kilogram, the unit of osmolality.
glossary.ketones: Acids made from fat breakdown when insulin is very low; minimal in HHS.
glossary.ketogenesis: Production of ketones in the liver from fatty acids.
glossary.lipolysis: Breakdown of stored fat into fatty acids; suppressed by small amounts of insulin.
glossary.relative insulin deficiency: Some insulin is present, but not enough for the body's needs.
glossary.osmotic diuresis: Loss of water in urine dragged by glucose that the kidneys cannot reabsorb.
glossary.volume depletion: Loss of circulating fluid, causing low BP and fast pulse.
glossary.pre-renal: Kidney impairment from poor blood flow to the kidneys, such as dehydration.
glossary.GCS: Glasgow Coma Scale, 3 to 15; measures conscious level.
glossary.mucous membranes: Moist linings such as the mouth; dry in dehydration.
glossary.cerebral oedema: Brain swelling; in HHS caused by water rushing back into brain cells during fast correction.
glossary.mannitol: Osmotic agent given IV to draw water out of a swollen brain.
glossary.hypertonic saline: Concentrated saline used to reduce cerebral oedema.
glossary.ITU: Intensive therapy unit, for patients needing organ support.
glossary.hyperviscosity: Thickened blood that flows sluggishly and clots more easily.
glossary.thrombosis: Formation of a blood clot inside a vessel.
glossary.VTE: Venous thromboembolism: deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism.
glossary.LMWH: Low molecular weight heparin, given to prevent clots.
glossary.0.9% saline: Isotonic sodium chloride solution; the first-line fluid in HHS.
glossary.fixed-rate insulin: IV insulin at a set dose per kg per hour; 0.05 units/kg/hour in HHS.
glossary.U&Es: Urea and electrolytes: sodium, potassium, urea and creatinine.
glossary.VBG: Venous blood gas: gives pH, bicarbonate, glucose and potassium quickly.
glossary.ABG: Arterial blood gas: pH, oxygen, CO2 and bicarbonate from an artery.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein: an inflammatory marker that rises in infection.
glossary.JBDS: Joint British Diabetes Societies, who publish the UK HHS and DKA guidelines.
glossary.precipitant: The trigger that tipped the patient into the emergency.
glossary.gliclazide: Sulfonylurea tablet that lowers glucose by making the pancreas release insulin.
glossary.metformin: First-line type 2 diabetes tablet; reduces liver glucose output.
